Under fixed robot supervision, RoboCasa performance improves monotonically as affordance-annotated human video scales. These results support affordance as an effective interface for both vision-language-action learning and human-to-robot transfer.

深圳市人工智能与机器人研究院 (AIRS).title: BlenderWorld: Benchmarking Visual Agents for 3D Creation from Real-World References
深圳市人工智能与机器人研究院 (AIRS).authors_text: Xinyu Fang, Yuchi Wang, Weihao Yu, Rongyao Fang, Zhaohai Li
深圳市人工智能与机器人研究院 (AIRS).summary: BlenderWorld introduces a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multimodal models in realistic 3D creation tasks, revealing significant challenges in spatial coherence and structural accuracy.
深圳市人工智能与机器人研究院 (AIRS).debug_abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have enabled them to act as autonomous agents, creating and editing 3D models via code or direct software manipulation. In practical workflows, these models must infer object shapes, materials, spatial layouts, and lighting from diverse references while strictly following instructions to reconstruct, modify, or design 3D content. However, existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of such open-ended requests across real-world scenarios. To bridge this gap, we introduce BlenderWorld, the first comprehensive benchmark dedicated to evaluating frontier models on realistic 3D creation tasks. BlenderWorld comprises 223 tasks spanning architecture, products, natural environments, and scientific visualization, driven by text, image, video, and structured specification inputs. To rigorously assess these complex deliverables, we establish a unified evaluation protocol: we render the submitted Blender projects from multiple viewpoints and evaluate them against 2,651 task-specific binary rubrics alongside holistic visual quality scores. Benchmarking thirteen frontier models reveals that GPT-6-Astra achieves the highest overall fused score of 79.9, followed by Opus-5 (73.0) and GPT-5.6-Sol (67.7). Ultimately, our findings reveal a critical bottleneck: while current models can parse broad instructions, they still profoundly struggle with fine-grained 3D spatial coherence and accurate structural reproduction in Blender, leaving substantial headroom for future 3D-native agentics.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: A Phenomenology of Neural Geometry in Vision-Language-Action Models
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Mozes Jacobs, Aiden Swann, Mathilde Papillon, Siddharth Boppana, Fenil R. Doshi
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: This paper explores the multi-dimensional geometric representations of task-relevant concepts in vision-language-action models, revealing their significance in robotic manipulation beyond mere readability.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Robotic manipulation is inherently geometric, but what shape does the world take inside the policy that performs it? Prior work on vision-language-action (VLA) policies establishes that task-relevant variables are linearly readable from activations, yet readability certifies only that a variable is present and says nothing about the shape its values trace, which may be curved and multi-dimensional. Using controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions, we build a taxonomy of seven task-relevant concepts in VLA models. We find that realized geometry is predominantly multi-dimensional and is shaped by the constraints under which the policy acts. Physical joint limits, for example, leave wrist orientation an open arc rather than a circle, and distance to the target, a single scalar, is realized in two orthogonal subspaces, a coarse ruler for the approach and a fine ruler for the grasp. The same geometries reappear in two further VLA models on real-world robot data, indicating that they are neither model-specific nor artifacts of simulation. We demonstrate how the findings are actionable by steering along the geometry a concept realizes. Overall, this work lays out an initial phenomenology of realized geometry in VLA policies and demonstrates that a concept's shape carries as much importance as its readability.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: Self-Supervised Inertial Odometry
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Yuheng Qiu, Yutian Chen, Carlton Cort, Weison Huang, Shibo Zhao
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: The paper presents a self-supervised method for training inertial odometry models without ground-truth trajectories, achieving high accuracy through myopic integration and pose graph distillation.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Learning inertial odometry for a new platform usually requires ground-truth trajectories. We show that an inertial odometry model can instead be trained from scratch by a myopic teacher that integrates the IMU over each short window independently, a scheme we call integration self-supervision.Interestingly, although supervised only by short-window velocity changes, the student learns to directly predict velocity, and does so more accurately than its integration teacher. Pose graph distillation then refines the model with sequence-consistent targets from a pose graph over many windows. 斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: Can LLM Agents Respond to Disasters? Benchmarking Heterogeneous Geospatial Reasoning in Emergency Operations

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Jifeng Wang, Kaouther Messaoud, Yuejiang Liu, Juergen Gall, Alexandre Alahi

Code is available at https://github.com/csjfwang/Forecast-PEFT.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Jingyi Xiang, Yixuan Wang, Jeannette Bohg, Wenzhen Yuan

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Contact-rich manipulation is essential to everyday activities, yet evaluating robots' ability to perform these activities remains challenging because of their diverse contact behaviors and the difficulty of reproducing tasks across laboratories. The benchmark is open-sourced at https://jingyi-xiang.github.io/contactbench

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Abstract Action-conditioned world models for contact-rich manipulation require data that captures how contact forms, slides, and releases under varying force. 斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: This paper explores the multi-dimensional geometric representations of task-relevant concepts in vision-language-action models, revealing their significance in robotic manipulation beyond mere readability.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Yuxiang Ma, Weihan Xu, Pengfei Ye, Anna Mei, Yuxin Ray Song
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: ACTS learns visuo-tactile world models from human interactions, enabling robots to predict contact dynamics more reliably than visual appearances in manipulation tasks.

ACTS jointly predicts future scene, wrist, and tactile observations. On held-out human data, ACTS improves scene-view prediction by 0.7-2.0 dB PSNR over the stronger of two visuo-tactile world models trained from scratch on React. Without fine-tuning, in the robot teleoperation rollouts we inspected, predicted tactile imprints still appear and disappear with recorded contact. Visual transfer is less robust: camera predictions exceed frame copying on PushT, are mixed on Rope, and fall below it on Motherboard, while wrist views can blur or hallucinate structure. These results suggest that contact dynamics transfer more reliably than visual appearance from human to robot.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: A Phenomenology of Neural Geometry in Vision-Language-Action Models
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Mozes Jacobs, Aiden Swann, Mathilde Papillon, Siddharth Boppana, Fenil R. Doshi
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: This paper explores the multi-dimensional geometric representations of task-relevant concepts in vision-language-action models, revealing their significance in robotic manipulation beyond mere readability.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Robotic manipulation is inherently geometric, but what shape does the world take inside the policy that performs it? Prior work on vision-language-action (VLA) policies establishes that task-relevant variables are linearly readable from activations, yet readability certifies only that a variable is present and says nothing about the shape its values trace, which may be curved and multi-dimensional. Using controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions, we build a taxonomy of seven task-relevant concepts in VLA models. We find that realized geometry is predominantly multi-dimensional and is shaped by the constraints under which the policy acts. Physical joint limits, for example, leave wrist orientation an open arc rather than a circle, and distance to the target, a single scalar, is realized in two orthogonal subspaces, a coarse ruler for the approach and a fine ruler for the grasp. The same geometries reappear in two further VLA models on real-world robot data, indicating that they are neither model-specific nor artifacts of simulation. We demonstrate how the findings are actionable by steering along the geometry a concept realizes. Overall, this work lays out an initial phenomenology of realized geometry in VLA policies and demonstrates that a concept's shape carries as much importance as its readability.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Self-Supervised Inertial Odometry
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Yuheng Qiu, Yutian Chen, Carlton Cort, Weison Huang, Shibo Zhao
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The paper presents a self-supervised method for training inertial odometry models without ground-truth trajectories, achieving high accuracy through myopic integration and pose graph distillation.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Learning inertial odometry for a new platform usually requires ground-truth trajectories. We show that an inertial odometry model can instead be trained from scratch by a myopic teacher that integrates the IMU over each short window independently, a scheme we call integration self-supervision.Interestingly, although supervised only by short-window velocity changes, the student learns to directly predict velocity, and does so more accurately than its integration teacher. Pose graph distillation then refines the model with sequence-consistent targets from a pose graph over many windows. Training on a new platform therefore no longer requires collecting ground-truth trajectories, but only calibrating the IMU and recording data during normal operation. Across six datasets spanning pedestrians, drones, quadrupeds, and a humanoid, the same recipe with no velocity or position labels trains models that come within $0.07$~m/s average velocity error of a same-architecture supervised baseline.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Long-Horizon Multi-Object Rearrangement via Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Kallol Saha, Yining Hong, Amber Li, Yejin Choi, Maxim Likhachev
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: DISCO introduces a method for long-horizon multi-object rearrangement by combining distilled tree search with continuous action policies, outperforming traditional approaches in both simulation and real-world tasks.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Despite recent advances in policy learning, long-horizon manipulation remains difficult because learned policies must avoid compounding errors while preserving future feasibility. While search-based planning can explicitly reason over such future consequences, it quickly becomes expensive in high-dimensional continuous action spaces. This raises a central question: how can long-horizon reasoning from search be transferred into policies in continuous action spaces? To this end, we propose DISCO: Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions. DISCO uses progressive-widening MCTS in physics simulation to generate long-horizon plans. During search, a learned policy proposes continuous actions, while a learned value function scores actions by their expected progress toward task completion. Using GPU-parallelized simulation, DISCO periodically distills MCTS-generated plans into the policy-value model, improving the action proposals and value estimates used in subsequent searches. Finally, the learned policy-value model can be directly deployed without the need for simulator-based search at test time. Across simulated and real-world rearrangement tasks, DISCO outperforms behavior cloning, reinforcement learning, and search-based baselines.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: SteerAct: Unlocking Action Models through Few-Shot Temporal Steering
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Kaichen Zhou, Zhiyan Li, Chongkai Gao, Yuhan Wang, Wenlong Huang
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: SteerAct enhances pretrained robot action models by using few-shot temporal steering to optimize feature activations, improving task success by 10% without weight updates.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Improving pretrained robot action models at test time from only a few rollouts remains challenging. Activation steering offers a lightweight approach by modifying feature activations while keeping model weights fixed. However, effective steering requires identifying which features to modify and determining the timing and strength of modification. We introduce SteerAct, a few-shot temporal steering framework that uses a shared temporal descriptor of sparse-feature dynamics for offline feature selection and online control. A pretrained sparse autoencoder provides candidate features, and our temporal descriptor summarizes the distribution of local activation-order patterns for each feature, enabling comparisons across rollouts without requiring timestep alignment. Before steering begins (offline), we use successful and failed reference rollouts to select a single task-specific feature whose temporal descriptors best distinguish the two outcomes and construct its reference banks. During each new execution (online), we compare the feature's evolving temporal descriptor with these references to determine when to intervene and how strongly to increase or decrease its activation via a steering coefficient. Using only 24 outcome-labeled rollouts per task, SteerAct improves task success by approximately 10% relative to unsteered models in evaluations spanning $π_{0.5}$, Fast-WAM, RoboTwin 2.0, DexJoCo, and real-world manipulation, without updating action-model weights. Code and demos are available at: https://steeract.github.io/.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Test-Time Hinting for Black-Box Vision-Language Models
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Kaihua Hou, Abhijith Varma Mudunuri, Jiaxing Qiu, Roxana Daneshjou, Thomas Hartvigsen
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: This paper introduces Test-Time Hinting, a method enhancing black-box vision-language model performance by providing targeted hints to mitigate common error patterns without model access.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) methods have proven highly effective for LLMs, yet their application to vision-language models (VLMs) remains relatively underexplored. Existing VLM TTS methods largely require open-weight model access or expensive repeated sampling, and are evaluated primarily on multimodal mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks rather than natural-image understanding. In this paper, we propose Test-Time Hinting, a method that improves VLM performance with a single call to the target VLM and requires only black-box API access, which makes it broadly applicable to frontier closed-weight models. Our method is motivated by the observation that VLM errors tend to cluster around recurring failure patterns that are shared across models and predictable from the input alone. We therefore train a lightweight hint generator model to predict, for a given test input, which "hint" should be prepended to the prompt, providing targeted contextual or procedural guidance that steers the VLM away from its characteristic failure modes without revealing the answer. We show that Test-Time Hinting significantly improves the accuracy of multiple closed-weight VLMs on natural-image VQA benchmarks and that these gains generalize to unseen benchmarks and VLMs without retraining the hint generator.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Dream What I Can: Sparse Visual Planning for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Chongkai Gao, Wenlong Huang, Haonan Chen, Lin Shao, Yilun Du
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: DreamCan introduces a hierarchical policy for robot manipulation that utilizes sparse visual planning to generate executable subgoals from video models, outperforming existing planning methods.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Video models provide rich priors for generalizable robotic manipulation, but plausible visual futures are not always executable. Additional suboptimal videos and test-time compute further improve success. The system also performs challenging real-world bimanual tasks, including box folding and packing with unseen object combinations. More results are available at https://dreamcan.github.io/.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Action-Aligned Latent Planning for Versatile Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Yutang Lin, Guanya Shi, C. Karen Liu
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The FIBER framework enables versatile humanoid loco-manipulation by integrating high-level planning with low-level control through a shared latent space, achieving significant performance improvements in diverse tasks.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Learning a single perceptive policy for diverse humanoid loco-manipulation requires unifying high-level task decisions without losing the state-dependent physical responses that make each interaction succeed. Across 128 diverse variations per task in simulation, FIBER achieves 42.0% mean success, more than tripling projected latent replay (11.6%) and substantially outperforming kinematic planning (3.5%). Real-world experiments further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer, skill chaining, and conditional steering through the same unified planner.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: SurGPT: A Multi-Task Foundation Model for Robotic Surgical Skills Assessment and Gesture Recognition
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Parham M. Kebria, Saeid Nahavandi, Mehrdad Saif, Fernando Bello
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: SurGPT is a multi-task foundation model that automates robotic surgical skills assessment and gesture recognition, enhancing training scalability and providing interpretable evaluations.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: The assessment of surgical skills in robotic surgery training has traditionally relied on subjective evaluations by human experts, creating bottlenecks in surgical education and limiting scalability. We present a novel foundation model that automatically analyzes robotic surgical videos to provide comprehensive skill assessment and gesture understanding. Combining a visual encoder with a transformer architecture, the model performs three key tasks simultaneously: 1) surgical task classification (knot tying, needle passing, suturing), 2) skill level assessment on a standardized scale, and 3) natural language generation of surgical gesture descriptions. The model processes video sequences from the da Vinci surgical robot and generates human-readable text descriptions of surgical actions, similar to how language models generate text from prompts, using a multi-task learning framework with adaptive uncertainty weighting to optimize performance across all objectives. Our transformer-based architecture incorporates positional encoding for temporal understanding and attention mechanisms for spatiotemporal feature integration. Evaluated on the da Vinci Skills Simulator dataset, the proposed framework demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in surgical task recognition and provides interpretable skill assessments that correlate with expert evaluations, with the model's ability to generate natural language descriptions of surgical gestures opening new possibilities for automated surgical education, real-time feedback systems, and objective skill assessment in surgical training and certification programs.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: MOIRA: Policy Memory and Belief Revision for Language-Model Agents in Non-Stationary Pair Trading
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Polydoros Giannouris, Yuechen Jiang, Lingfei Qian, Yuyan Wang, Xueqing Peng
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: The paper presents MOIRA, a language-driven hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for pair trading that optimizes high-level and low-level policies using large language models, enhancing decision-making under non-stationarity.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Many sequential decision-making problems exhibit hierarchical structure, where high-level semantic choices constrain downstream actions and feedback is delayed and ambiguous. Learning in such settings is challenging due to credit assignment: performance degradation may arise from flawed abstractions, suboptimal execution, or their interaction. We study this challenge through pair trading, a domain that naturally combines long-horizon semantic reasoning for asset pair selection with short-horizon execution under partial observability. We formulate pair trading as a hierarchical reinforcement learning problem and propose a language-driven optimization framework in which both high-level and low-level policies are parameterized by large language models (LLMs) and optimized exclusively through prompt updates. Our approach leverages pretrained LLMs as hierarchical policies and uses trajectory- and episode-level textual feedback to adapt abstractions and execution without gradient-based fine-tuning. By explicitly separating abstraction selection from execution, the framework reduces non-stationarity across hierarchical levels and enables targeted adaptation under delayed feedback. Experiments on real-world market data show consistent improvements over traditional and LLM-based baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of language-driven hierarchical reinforcement learning.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Learning Self-Orchestration in Decentralized Agent Swarms
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Guowei Xu, Zhenting Qi, Amani Kiruga, Himabindu Lakkaraju, Yilun Du
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: The paper presents a market-based post-training framework that enables decentralized agent swarms to jointly learn action policies and self-orchestration, enhancing adaptability and performance.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Yet existing multi-agent systems often train agents within fixed orchestration structures, separating the learning of individual capabilities from the organization of collective behavior. We introduce market-based post-training (MPT), a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Agents express their willingness to participate through bids, which determine who acts and how collective outcomes provide local training credit. Learning both action and bidding behavior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate MPT on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post-training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alternative coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robustness in decentralized agent swarms. More details are available on our project page at https://guoweixu.com/mpt/.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: SteerAct: Unlocking Action Models through Few-Shot Temporal Steering
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Kaichen Zhou, Zhiyan Li, Chongkai Gao, Yuhan Wang, Wenlong Huang
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: SteerAct enhances pretrained robot action models by using few-shot temporal steering to optimize feature activations, improving task success by 10% without weight updates.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Improving pretrained robot action models at test time from only a few rollouts remains challenging. Activation steering offers a lightweight approach by modifying feature activations while keeping model weights fixed. However, effective steering requires identifying which features to modify and determining the timing and strength of modification. We introduce SteerAct, a few-shot temporal steering framework that uses a shared temporal descriptor of sparse-feature dynamics for offline feature selection and online control. A pretrained sparse autoencoder provides candidate features, and our temporal descriptor summarizes the distribution of local activation-order patterns for each feature, enabling comparisons across rollouts without requiring timestep alignment. Before steering begins (offline), we use successful and failed reference rollouts to select a single task-specific feature whose temporal descriptors best distinguish the two outcomes and construct its reference banks. During each new execution (online), we compare the feature's evolving temporal descriptor with these references to determine when to intervene and how strongly to increase or decrease its activation via a steering coefficient. Rajpurkar Lab.title: Learning When to Abort in Transformer Planning: A Mechanistic Study
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Shi Feng, Qimin Zhong, Siwei Wang, Yifei Shen, Shang-Hua Teng
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: This study explores error detection in Transformer planning by training models to recognize invalid transitions, enhancing planning reliability through abort mechanisms and retry strategies.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Planning does not by itself imply the ability to recognise errors, but recognising errors can improve planning capacity. In this paper, we study this phenomenon in Transformer planning. To analyze the inner mechanism, we follow the approach of Wang et al. (2024) and abstract planning as path-finding in graphs. In this setting, we train the model to detect the error of invalid transitions, i.e., after the model generates a next node that is not adjacent with the current node, the model should then generate a special abort token x. For expressiveness, we construct a Transformer with feed-forward width $O(|V|)$ for any fixed graph with node set $V$. It can detect all possible invalid transitions, and select a valid next node if the prefix is valid. We then propose a worst-case lower bound on feed-forward width, which makes the detector's linear width near-optimal up to logarithmic factors. In trained models, we demonstrate that invalid-transition detection increases previous-node attention, and most of the valid--invalid separation locates in the feed-forward network's output. This accords with our theoretical insights. Finally, we use this error detection to improve the model's performance: at inference, generating the abort token x will directly cause an external procedure to discard the attempt and restart from the original prompt. Rajpurkar Lab.title: Dream What I Can: Sparse Visual Planning for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Chongkai Gao, Wenlong Huang, Haonan Chen, Lin Shao, Yilun Du
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: DreamCan introduces a hierarchical policy for robot manipulation that utilizes sparse visual planning to generate executable subgoals from video models, outperforming existing planning methods.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Video models provide rich priors for generalizable robotic manipulation, but plausible visual futures are not always executable. We introduce DreamCan, a hierarchical policy that grounds video models through sparse visual planning: a high-level planner adapted from a pre-trained video model and a low-level visuomotor policy. Rather than predicting dense trajectories, the high-level planner generates sparse visual subgoals that balance reachability and task utility. From offline, action-free robot videos, we estimate these quantities and use dynamic programming to select subgoal sequences without manual annotations. The resulting subgoals are more reliably attained than uniformly spaced alternatives, and the full system outperforms language, dense-video, and uniform-subgoal planners, reaching high planning success rates on Language-Table tasks and 91.2% success on LIBERO-Long with a 0.1B-parameter low-level policy. Additional suboptimal videos and test-time compute further improve success. The system also performs challenging real-world bimanual tasks, including box folding and packing with unseen object combinations. More results are available at https://dreamcan.github.io/.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: ACTS: Learning Visuo-Tactile World Models from Human Physical Interaction
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Yuxiang Ma, Weihan Xu, Pengfei Ye, Anna Mei, Yuxin Ray Song
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: ACTS learns visuo-tactile world models from human interactions, enabling robots to predict contact dynamics more reliably than visual appearances in manipulation tasks.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Abstract Action-conditioned world models for contact-rich manipulation require data that captures how contact forms, slides, and releases under varying force. Such data are slow to collect through robot teleoperation, which often lacks force feedback and is constrained by gripper geometry. We ask whether these dynamics can instead be learned from human physical interaction and transferred to a robot. We present ACTS, a visuo-tactile world model trained only on human interaction data. Operators manipulate handheld GelSight sensors while we record third-person and wrist video, tactile images, 6-DoF sensor motion, and tactile-derived normal force, yielding React, a 4.9-hour bimanual dataset across three objects. We represent actions at the tactile sensor as motion augmented by force change, providing a shared action space for human collection and robot execution. Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: A Phenomenology of Neural Geometry in Vision-Language-Action Models
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Mozes Jacobs, Aiden Swann, Mathilde Papillon, Siddharth Boppana, Fenil R. Doshi
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: This paper explores the multi-dimensional geometric representations of task-relevant concepts in vision-language-action models, revealing their significance in robotic manipulation beyond mere readability.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Self-Supervised Inertial Odometry
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Yuheng Qiu, Yutian Chen, Carlton Cort, Weison Huang, Shibo Zhao
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The paper presents a self-supervised method for training inertial odometry models without ground-truth trajectories, achieving high accuracy through myopic integration and pose graph distillation.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Learning inertial odometry for a new platform usually requires ground-truth trajectories. We show that an inertial odometry model can instead be trained from scratch by a myopic teacher that integrates the IMU over each short window independently, a scheme we call integration self-supervision.Interestingly, although supervised only by short-window velocity changes, the student learns to directly predict velocity, and does so more accurately than its integration teacher. Pose graph distillation then refines the model with sequence-consistent targets from a pose graph over many windows. Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Long-Horizon Multi-Object Rearrangement via Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Kallol Saha, Yining Hong, Amber Li, Yejin Choi, Maxim Likhachev
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: DISCO introduces a method for long-horizon multi-object rearrangement by combining distilled tree search with continuous action policies, outperforming traditional approaches in both simulation and real-world tasks.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Despite recent advances in policy learning, long-horizon manipulation remains difficult because learned policies must avoid compounding errors while preserving future feasibility. While search-based planning can explicitly reason over such future consequences, it quickly becomes expensive in high-dimensional continuous action spaces. This raises a central question: how can long-horizon reasoning from search be transferred into policies in continuous action spaces? To this end, we propose DISCO: Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions. DISCO uses progressive-widening MCTS in physics simulation to generate long-horizon plans. During search, a learned policy proposes continuous actions, while a learned value function scores actions by their expected progress toward task completion. Using GPU-parallelized simulation, DISCO periodically distills MCTS-generated plans into the policy-value model, improving the action proposals and value estimates used in subsequent searches. Finally, the learned policy-value model can be directly deployed without the need for simulator-based search at test time. Across simulated and real-world rearrangement tasks, DISCO outperforms behavior cloning, reinforcement learning, and search-based baselines.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Test-Time Hinting for Black-Box Vision-Language Models
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Kaihua Hou, Abhijith Varma Mudunuri, Jiaxing Qiu, Roxana Daneshjou, Thomas Hartvigsen
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: This paper introduces Test-Time Hinting, a method enhancing black-box vision-language model performance by providing targeted hints to mitigate common error patterns without model access.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) methods have proven highly effective for LLMs, yet their application to vision-language models (VLMs) remains relatively underexplored. Existing VLM TTS methods largely require open-weight model access or expensive repeated sampling, and are evaluated primarily on multimodal mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks rather than natural-image understanding. Our method is motivated by the observation that VLM errors tend to cluster around recurring failure patterns that are shared across models and predictable from the input alone. We therefore train a lightweight hint generator model to predict, for a given test input, which "hint" should be prepended to the prompt, providing targeted contextual or procedural guidance that steers the VLM away from its characteristic failure modes without revealing the answer. We show that Test-Time Hinting significantly improves the accuracy of multiple closed-weight VLMs on natural-image VQA benchmarks and that these gains generalize to unseen benchmarks and VLMs without retraining the hint generator.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Action-Aligned Latent Planning for Versatile Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Yutang Lin, Guanya Shi, C. Karen Liu
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The FIBER framework enables versatile humanoid loco-manipulation by integrating high-level planning with low-level control through a shared latent space, achieving significant performance improvements in diverse tasks.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Learning a single perceptive policy for diverse humanoid loco-manipulation requires unifying high-level task decisions without losing the state-dependent physical responses that make each interaction succeed. This makes the representation between high-level planning and whole-body control critical: kinematic or contact targets provide compact abstractions but do not directly encode interaction-specific control responses, while directly predicting low-level actions requires the planner to model high-frequency closed-loop feedback. We propose FIBER, a framework that uses the executable latent space of a frozen behavioral foundation model (BFM) as a shared planning representation for heterogeneous interaction skills. Our latent policy projection (LPP) maps independently acquired task-specific policies into this representation by identifying latent commands whose induced actions match their local control responses, enabling lower-rate planning while retaining the BFM's high-frequency state feedback. After projection, we aggregate closed-loop latent rollouts from all skills and train a single perceptive flow planner entirely offline. We further introduce AH-BFM, an adaptive-horizon BFM trained with multi-gamma forward-backward (FB) learning to support both precise control and temporally extended whole-body behavior. We evaluate FIBER on box pickup, door opening, and object grasping in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid. Across 128 diverse variations per task in simulation, FIBER achieves 42.0% mean success, more than tripling projected latent replay (11.6%) and substantially outperforming kinematic planning (3.5%). Real-world experiments further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer, skill chaining, and conditional steering through the same unified planner.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Can LLM Agents Respond to Disasters? Benchmarking Heterogeneous Geospatial Reasoning in Emergency Operations
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Junjue Wang, Weihao Xuan, Heli Qi, Pengyu Dai, Kunyi Liu
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The paper introduces DORA, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents in end-to-end disaster response, highlighting challenges in grounding, tool selection, and compositional fragility.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Operational disaster response goes beyond damage assessment, requiring responders to integrate multi-sensor signals, reason over road networks, populations and key facilities, plan evacuations, and produce actionable reports. However, prior work largely isolates remote-sensing perception or evaluates generic tool use, leaving the end-to-end workflows of emergency operations underexplored. In this paper, we introduce Disaster Operational Response Agent benchmark (DORA), the first agentic benchmark for end-to-end disaster response: 515 expert-authored tasks across 45 real-world disaster events spanning 10 types, paired with expert-verified, replayable gold trajectories totaling 3,500 tool-call steps. Tasks span five dimensions that cover the operational disaster-response pipeline: disaster perception, spatial relational analysis, rescue and evacuation planning, temporal evolution reasoning, and multi-modal report synthesis. Agents compose calls from a 108-tool MCP library over heterogeneous geospatial data: optical, SAR, and multi-spectral imagery across single-, bi-, and multi-temporal sequences (0.015-10m GSD), complemented by elevation and social vector layers. We comprehensively evaluate 13 frontier LLMs on our benchmark, revealing three persistent challenges: 1) disaster-domain grounding exposes unique failure modes (damage-semantic grounding, sensor-modality mismatch, and disaster-pipeline composition); 2) agents are doubly bottlenecked by tool selection and argument grounding, where gold tool-order hints improve accuracy by only 1.08-4.40%, and alternative scaffolds yield at most a 3.24% gain; 3) compositional fragility scales with trajectory length, the agent-to-gold gap widening from 7% to 56% on long pipelines. DORA establishes a rigorous testbed for operationally reliable disaster-response agents. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Junjue-Wang/DORA.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Forecast-PEFT: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Pre-trained Motion Forecasting Models
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Jifeng Wang, Kaouther Messaoud, Yuejiang Liu, Juergen Gall, Alexandre Alahi
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: Forecast-PEFT introduces a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for motion forecasting that significantly reduces retraining needs while enhancing accuracy compared to traditional approaches.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Recent advancements in motion forecasting have been significantly accelerated by self-supervised pre-training techniques. However, current methods typically rely on extensive fine-tuning of pre-trained models for downstream tasks like trajectory prediction, a process that can be inefficient. This inefficiency primarily arises because traditional fine-tuning strategies fail to fully exploit the close alignment between motion prediction tasks and masked reconstruction objectives used during pre-training. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Forecast-PEFT, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework specifically designed for motion forecasting. Forecast-PEFT preserves most of the pre-trained model's parameters, introducing minimal yet effective adjustments through novel prompts and adapters. By doing so, Forecast-PEFT significantly reduces the number of parameters needing retraining while preserving essential pre-trained knowledge. Our method demonstrates robust generalization across multiple datasets, achieving higher accuracy with only about 17% of the parameters required by traditional full fine-tuning approaches. Additionally, our fully fine-tuned variant, Forecast-FT, further enhances prediction performance, achieving improvements of up to 9.6% over conventional baseline methods. These findings highlight Forecast-PEFT as a scalable, efficient, and effective alternative for fine-tuning pre-trained motion forecasting models. Code is available at https://github.com/csjfwang/Forecast-PEFT.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: ContactBench 1.0: A Benchmark for Everyday Contact-Rich Robotic Manipulation
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Jingyi Xiang, Yixuan Wang, Jeannette Bohg, Wenzhen Yuan
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: ContactBench 1.0 is an open-source benchmark for evaluating contact-rich robotic manipulation through 36 tasks and 40+ object assets, highlighting challenges in policy performance.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Contact-rich manipulation is essential to everyday activities, yet evaluating robots' ability to perform these activities remains challenging because of their diverse contact behaviors and the difficulty of reproducing tasks across laboratories. Drawing on observations of everyday human manipulation, we identify eight recurring skill categories that provide a practical framework for studying these capabilities. The assets capture task-relevant geometry and contact behavior, support reproducible fabrication using consumer-grade 3D printers, and are paired with simulation models with tunable resistance loads. Controlled task variations enable evaluation of policy generalization. We evaluate recent vision-based and vision-tactile policy learning methods on six benchmark tasks. The results reveal that the evaluated vision-only policies struggle to perceive or react to contact events, while the evaluated visual-tactile policies do not meaningfully improve performance. By providing shared tasks and physical and simulated assets, ContactBench 1.0 establishes a foundation for reproducible evaluation of contact-rich manipulation research. The benchmark is open-sourced at https://jingyi-xiang.github.io/contactbench

斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).authors_text: Kaihua Hou, Abhijith Varma Mudunuri, Jiaxing Qiu, Roxana Daneshjou, Thomas Hartvigsen
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).summary: This paper introduces Test-Time Hinting, a method enhancing black-box vision-language model performance by providing targeted hints to mitigate common error patterns without model access.
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).debug_abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) methods have proven highly effective for LLMs, yet their application to vision-language models (VLMs) remains relatively underexplored. Existing VLM TTS methods largely require open-weight model access or expensive repeated sampling, and are evaluated primarily on multimodal mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks rather than natural-image understanding. In this paper, we propose Test-Time Hinting, a method that improves VLM performance with a single call to the target VLM and requires only black-box API access, which makes it broadly applicable to frontier closed-weight models. Our method is motivated by the observation that VLM errors tend to cluster around recurring failure patterns that are shared across models and predictable from the input alone. We therefore train a lightweight hint generator model to predict, for a given test input, which "hint" should be prepended to the prompt, providing targeted contextual or procedural guidance that steers the VLM away from its characteristic failure modes without revealing the answer. We show that Test-Time Hinting significantly improves the accuracy of multiple closed-weight VLMs on natural-image VQA benchmarks and that these gains generalize to unseen benchmarks and VLMs without retraining the hint generator.

斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).title: Dream What I Can: Sparse Visual Planning for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).authors_text: Chongkai Gao, Wenlong Huang, Haonan Chen, Lin Shao, Yilun Du
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).summary: DreamCan introduces a hierarchical policy for robot manipulation that utilizes sparse visual planning to generate executable subgoals from video models, outperforming existing planning methods.
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).debug_abstract: Video models provide rich priors for generalizable robotic manipulation, but plausible visual futures are not always executable. We introduce DreamCan, a hierarchical policy that grounds video models through sparse visual planning: a high-level planner adapted from a pre-trained video model and a low-level visuomotor policy. Rather than predicting dense trajectories, the high-level planner generates sparse visual subgoals that balance reachability and task utility. From offline, action-free robot videos, we estimate these quantities and use dynamic programming to select subgoal sequences without manual annotations. The resulting subgoals are more reliably attained than uniformly spaced alternatives, and the full system outperforms language, dense-video, and uniform-subgoal planners, reaching high planning success rates on Language-Table tasks and 91.2% success on LIBERO-Long with a 0.1B-parameter low-level policy. Additional suboptimal videos and test-time compute further improve success. The system also performs challenging real-world bimanual tasks, including box folding and packing with unseen object combinations. More results are available at https://dreamcan.github.io/.

斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).title: Action-Aligned Latent Planning for Versatile Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).authors_text: Yutang Lin, Guanya Shi, C. Karen Liu
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).summary: The FIBER framework enables versatile humanoid loco-manipulation by integrating high-level planning with low-level control through a shared latent space, achieving significant performance improvements in diverse tasks.
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).debug_abstract: Learning a single perceptive policy for diverse humanoid loco-manipulation requires unifying high-level task decisions without losing the state-dependent physical responses that make each interaction succeed. This makes the representation between high-level planning and whole-body control critical: kinematic or contact targets provide compact abstractions but do not directly encode interaction-specific control responses, while directly predicting low-level actions requires the planner to model high-frequency closed-loop feedback. We propose FIBER, a framework that uses the executable latent space of a frozen behavioral foundation model (BFM) as a shared planning representation for heterogeneous interaction skills. Our latent policy projection (LPP) maps independently acquired task-specific policies into this representation by identifying latent commands whose induced actions match their local control responses, enabling lower-rate planning while retaining the BFM's high-frequency state feedback. After projection, we aggregate closed-loop latent rollouts from all skills and train a single perceptive flow planner entirely offline. We further introduce AH-BFM, an adaptive-horizon BFM trained with multi-gamma forward-backward (FB) learning to support both precise control and temporally extended whole-body behavior. We evaluate FIBER on box pickup, door opening, and object grasping in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid. Across 128 diverse variations per task in simulation, FIBER achieves 42.0% mean success, more than tripling projected latent replay (11.6%) and substantially outperforming kinematic planning (3.5%). Real-world experiments further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer, skill chaining, and conditional steering through the same unified planner.

斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).title: Can LLM Agents Respond to Disasters? Benchmarking Heterogeneous Geospatial Reasoning in Emergency Operations
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).authors_text: Junjue Wang, Weihao Xuan, Heli Qi, Pengyu Dai, Kunyi Liu
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).summary: The paper introduces DORA, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents in end-to-end disaster response, highlighting challenges in grounding, tool selection, and compositional fragility.
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).debug_abstract: Operational disaster response goes beyond damage assessment, requiring responders to integrate multi-sensor signals, reason over road networks, populations and key facilities, plan evacuations, and produce actionable reports. However, prior work largely isolates remote-sensing perception or evaluates generic tool use, leaving the end-to-end workflows of emergency operations underexplored. In this paper, we introduce Disaster Operational Response Agent benchmark (DORA), the first agentic benchmark for end-to-end disaster response: 515 expert-authored tasks across 45 real-world disaster events spanning 10 types, paired with expert-verified, replayable gold trajectories totaling 3,500 tool-call steps. Tasks span five dimensions that cover the operational disaster-response pipeline: disaster perception, spatial relational analysis, rescue and evacuation planning, temporal evolution reasoning, and multi-modal report synthesis. Agents compose calls from a 108-tool MCP library over heterogeneous geospatial data: optical, SAR, and multi-spectral imagery across single-, bi-, and multi-temporal sequences (0.015-10m GSD), complemented by elevation and social vector layers. We comprehensively evaluate 13 frontier LLMs on our benchmark, revealing three persistent challenges: 1) disaster-domain grounding exposes unique failure modes (damage-semantic grounding, sensor-modality mismatch, and disaster-pipeline composition); 2) agents are doubly bottlenecked by tool selection and argument grounding, where gold tool-order hints improve accuracy by only 1.08-4.40%, and alternative scaffolds yield at most a 3.24% gain; 3) compositional fragility scales with trajectory length, the agent-to-gold gap widening from 7% to 56% on long pipelines. DORA establishes a rigorous testbed for operationally reliable disaster-response agents. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Junjue-Wang/DORA.

斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).title: Forecast-PEFT: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Pre-trained Motion Forecasting Models
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).authors_text: Jifeng Wang, Kaouther Messaoud, Yuejiang Liu, Juergen Gall, Alexandre Alahi
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).summary: Forecast-PEFT introduces a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for motion forecasting that significantly reduces retraining needs while enhancing accuracy compared to traditional approaches.
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).debug_abstract: Recent advancements in motion forecasting have been significantly accelerated by self-supervised pre-training techniques. However, current methods typically rely on extensive fine-tuning of pre-trained models for downstream tasks like trajectory prediction, a process that can be inefficient. This inefficiency primarily arises because traditional fine-tuning strategies fail to fully exploit the close alignment between motion prediction tasks and masked reconstruction objectives used during pre-training. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Forecast-PEFT, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework specifically designed for motion forecasting. Forecast-PEFT preserves most of the pre-trained model's parameters, introducing minimal yet effective adjustments through novel prompts and adapters. By doing so, Forecast-PEFT significantly reduces the number of parameters needing retraining while preserving essential pre-trained knowledge. Our method demonstrates robust generalization across multiple datasets, achieving higher accuracy with only about 17% of the parameters required by traditional full fine-tuning approaches. Additionally, our fully fine-tuned variant, Forecast-FT, further enhances prediction performance, achieving improvements of up to 9.6% over conventional baseline methods. These findings highlight Forecast-PEFT as a scalable, efficient, and effective alternative for fine-tuning pre-trained motion forecasting models. Code is available at https://github.com/csjfwang/Forecast-PEFT.

斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).title: ContactBench 1.0: A Benchmark for Everyday Contact-Rich Robotic Manipulation
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).authors_text: Jingyi Xiang, Yixuan Wang, Jeannette Bohg, Wenzhen Yuan
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).summary: ContactBench 1.0 is an open-source benchmark for evaluating contact-rich robotic manipulation through 36 tasks and 40+ object assets, highlighting challenges in policy performance.
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).debug_abstract: Contact-rich manipulation is essential to everyday activities, yet evaluating robots' ability to perform these activities remains challenging because of their diverse contact behaviors and the difficulty of reproducing tasks across laboratories. Drawing on observations of everyday human manipulation, we identify eight recurring skill categories that provide a practical framework for studying these capabilities. We introduce ContactBench 1.0, an extensible benchmark that instantiates these skills through 36 reference tasks and more than 40 object assets. The assets capture task-relevant geometry and contact behavior, support reproducible fabrication using consumer-grade 3D printers, and are paired with simulation models with tunable resistance loads. Controlled task variations enable evaluation of policy generalization. We evaluate recent vision-based and vision-tactile policy learning methods on six benchmark tasks. The results reveal that the evaluated vision-only policies struggle to perceive or react to contact events, while the evaluated visual-tactile policies do not meaningfully improve performance. By providing shared tasks and physical and simulated assets, ContactBench 1.0 establishes a foundation for reproducible evaluation of contact-rich manipulation research. The benchmark is open-sourced at https://jingyi-xiang.github.io/contactbench

斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).title: ACTS: Learning Visuo-Tactile World Models from Human Physical Interaction
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).authors_text: Yuxiang Ma, Weihan Xu, Pengfei Ye, Anna Mei, Yuxin Ray Song
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).summary: ACTS learns visuo-tactile world models from human interactions, enabling robots to predict contact dynamics more reliably than visual appearances in manipulation tasks.
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).debug_abstract: Abstract Action-conditioned world models for contact-rich manipulation require data that captures how contact forms, slides, and releases under varying force. Such data are slow to collect through robot teleoperation, which often lacks force feedback and is constrained by gripper geometry. We ask whether these dynamics can instead be learned from human physical interaction and transferred to a robot. We present ACTS, a visuo-tactile world model trained only on human interaction data. Operators manipulate handheld GelSight sensors while we record third-person and wrist video, tactile images, 6-DoF sensor motion, and tactile-derived normal force, yielding React, a 4.9-hour bimanual dataset across three objects. We represent actions at the tactile sensor as motion augmented by force change, providing a shared action space for human collection and robot execution. ACTS jointly predicts future scene, wrist, and tactile observations. On held-out human data, ACTS improves scene-view prediction by 0.7-2.0 dB PSNR over the stronger of two visuo-tactile world models trained from scratch on React. Without fine-tuning, in the robot teleoperation rollouts we inspected, predicted tactile imprints still appear and disappear with recorded contact. Visual transfer is less robust: camera predictions exceed frame copying on PushT, are mixed on Rope, and fall below it on Motherboard, while wrist views can blur or hallucinate structure. These results suggest that contact dynamics transfer more reliably than visual appearance from human to robot.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: SurGPT: A Multi-Task Foundation Model for Robotic Surgical Skills Assessment and Gesture Recognition
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Parham M. Kebria, Saeid Nahavandi, Mehrdad Saif, Fernando Bello
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: SurGPT is a multi-task foundation model that automates robotic surgical skills assessment and gesture recognition, enhancing training scalability and providing interpretable evaluations.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: The assessment of surgical skills in robotic surgery training has traditionally relied on subjective evaluations by human experts, creating bottlenecks in surgical education and limiting scalability. We present a novel foundation model that automatically analyzes robotic surgical videos to provide comprehensive skill assessment and gesture understanding. Combining a visual encoder with a transformer architecture, the model performs three key tasks simultaneously: 1) surgical task classification (knot tying, needle passing, suturing), 2) skill level assessment on a standardized scale, and 3) natural language generation of surgical gesture descriptions. The model processes video sequences from the da Vinci surgical robot and generates human-readable text descriptions of surgical actions, similar to how language models generate text from prompts, using a multi-task learning framework with adaptive uncertainty weighting to optimize performance across all objectives. Our transformer-based architecture incorporates positional encoding for temporal understanding and attention mechanisms for spatiotemporal feature integration. Evaluated on the da Vinci Skills Simulator dataset, the proposed framework demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in surgical task recognition and provides interpretable skill assessments that correlate with expert evaluations, with the model's ability to generate natural language descriptions of surgical gestures opening new possibilities for automated surgical education, real-time feedback systems, and objective skill assessment in surgical training and certification programs.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: A Phenomenology of Neural Geometry in Vision-Language-Action Models
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Mozes Jacobs, Aiden Swann, Mathilde Papillon, Siddharth Boppana, Fenil R. Doshi
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: This paper explores the multi-dimensional geometric representations of task-relevant concepts in vision-language-action models, revealing their significance in robotic manipulation beyond mere readability.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Robotic manipulation is inherently geometric, but what shape does the world take inside the policy that performs it? Prior work on vision-language-action (VLA) policies establishes that task-relevant variables are linearly readable from activations, yet readability certifies only that a variable is present and says nothing about the shape its values trace, which may be curved and multi-dimensional. Using controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions, we build a taxonomy of seven task-relevant concepts in VLA models. We find that realized geometry is predominantly multi-dimensional and is shaped by the constraints under which the policy acts. Physical joint limits, for example, leave wrist orientation an open arc rather than a circle, and distance to the target, a single scalar, is realized in two orthogonal subspaces, a coarse ruler for the approach and a fine ruler for the grasp. The same geometries reappear in two further VLA models on real-world robot data, indicating that they are neither model-specific nor artifacts of simulation. We demonstrate how the findings are actionable by steering along the geometry a concept realizes. Overall, this work lays out an initial phenomenology of realized geometry in VLA policies and demonstrates that a concept's shape carries as much importance as its readability.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: MOIRA: Policy Memory and Belief Revision for Language-Model Agents in Non-Stationary Pair Trading
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Polydoros Giannouris, Yuechen Jiang, Lingfei Qian, Yuyan Wang, Xueqing Peng
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: The paper presents MOIRA, a language-driven hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for pair trading that optimizes high-level and low-level policies using large language models, enhancing decision-making under non-stationarity.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Many sequential decision-making problems exhibit hierarchical structure, where high-level semantic choices constrain downstream actions and feedback is delayed and ambiguous. Learning in such settings is challenging due to credit assignment: performance degradation may arise from flawed abstractions, suboptimal execution, or their interaction. We study this challenge through pair trading, a domain that naturally combines long-horizon semantic reasoning for asset pair selection with short-horizon execution under partial observability. We formulate pair trading as a hierarchical reinforcement learning problem and propose a language-driven optimization framework in which both high-level and low-level policies are parameterized by large language models (LLMs) and optimized exclusively through prompt updates. Our approach leverages pretrained LLMs as hierarchical policies and uses trajectory- and episode-level textual feedback to adapt abstractions and execution without gradient-based fine-tuning. By explicitly separating abstraction selection from execution, the framework reduces non-stationarity across hierarchical levels and enables targeted adaptation under delayed feedback. Experiments on real-world market data show consistent improvements over traditional and LLM-based baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of language-driven hierarchical reinforcement learning.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: Learning Self-Orchestration in Decentralized Agent Swarms
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Guowei Xu, Zhenting Qi, Amani Kiruga, Himabindu Lakkaraju, Yilun Du
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: The paper presents a market-based post-training framework that enables decentralized agent swarms to jointly learn action policies and self-orchestration, enhancing adaptability and performance.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Yet existing multi-agent systems often train agents within fixed orchestration structures, separating the learning of individual capabilities from the organization of collective behavior. We introduce market-based post-training (MPT), a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Agents express their willingness to participate through bids, which determine who acts and how collective outcomes provide local training credit. Learning both action and bidding behavior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate MPT on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post-training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alternative coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robustness in decentralized agent swarms. More details are available on our project page at https://guoweixu.com/mpt/.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: SteerAct: Unlocking Action Models through Few-Shot Temporal Steering
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Kaichen Zhou, Zhiyan Li, Chongkai Gao, Yuhan Wang, Wenlong Huang
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: SteerAct enhances pretrained robot action models by using few-shot temporal steering to optimize feature activations, improving task success by 10% without weight updates.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Improving pretrained robot action models at test time from only a few rollouts remains challenging. Activation steering offers a lightweight approach by modifying feature activations while keeping model weights fixed. However, effective steering requires identifying which features to modify and determining the timing and strength of modification. We introduce SteerAct, a few-shot temporal steering framework that uses a shared temporal descriptor of sparse-feature dynamics for offline feature selection and online control. A pretrained sparse autoencoder provides candidate features, and our temporal descriptor summarizes the distribution of local activation-order patterns for each feature, enabling comparisons across rollouts without requiring timestep alignment. Before steering begins (offline), we use successful and failed reference rollouts to select a single task-specific feature whose temporal descriptors best distinguish the two outcomes and construct its reference banks. During each new execution (online), we compare the feature's evolving temporal descriptor with these references to determine when to intervene and how strongly to increase or decrease its activation via a steering coefficient. Using only 24 outcome-labeled rollouts per task, SteerAct improves task success by approximately 10% relative to unsteered models in evaluations spanning $π_{0.5}$, Fast-WAM, RoboTwin 2.0, DexJoCo, and real-world manipulation, without updating action-model weights. Code and demos are available at: https://steeract.github.io/.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: Learning When to Abort in Transformer Planning: A Mechanistic Study
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Shi Feng, Qimin Zhong, Siwei Wang, Yifei Shen, Shang-Hua Teng
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: This study explores error detection in Transformer planning by training models to recognize invalid transitions, enhancing planning reliability through abort mechanisms and retry strategies.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Planning does not by itself imply the ability to recognise errors, but recognising errors can improve planning capacity. In this paper, we study this phenomenon in Transformer planning. To analyze the inner mechanism, we follow the approach of Wang et al. (2024) and abstract planning as path-finding in graphs. In this setting, we train the model to detect the error of invalid transitions, i.e., after the model generates a next node that is not adjacent with the current node, the model should then generate a special abort token x. For expressiveness, we construct a Transformer with feed-forward width $O(|V|)$ for any fixed graph with node set $V$. It can detect all possible invalid transitions, and select a valid next node if the prefix is valid. We then propose a worst-case lower bound on feed-forward width, which makes the detector's linear width near-optimal up to logarithmic factors. In trained models, we demonstrate that invalid-transition detection increases previous-node attention, and most of the valid--invalid separation locates in the feed-forward network's output. This accords with our theoretical insights. Finally, we use this error detection to improve the model's performance: at inference, generating the abort token x will directly cause an external procedure to discard the attempt and restart from the original prompt. Experiments show that error detection combined with retry improves model's planning reliability on graphs, Countdown, and mazes.
